# Intersectional Demographic Trends in Infective Endocarditis Among Adults in the US, 2012–2021

KEY WORDS:  descriptive epidemiology; health disparities; infectious disease

J Gen Intern Med 41(4):1178–80 DOI: 10.1007/s11606-025-09872-1 © The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Society of General Internal Medicine 2025

## BACKGROUND

The estimated number of people who use injection drugs in the US has more than quadrupled since 2010. Injecting drugs places individuals at risk for infectious diseases that result from viruses and bacteria entering the bloodstream when using non-sterile paraphernalia. One serious sequalae is infective endocarditis (IE), an infection of the endocardium of the heart commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus, for which incidence has risen substantially in recent years.1 Prior epidemiologic work has found IE hospitalizations associated with injection drug use were highest among people who were younger, male, White, and had lower incomes.1 However, the previous research examined hospitalizations by singular sociodemographic categories, potentially masking subgroup heterogeneity.

Objective

This descriptive study characterizes IE hospitalizations among adults aged 18–64 living in 12 US states by the intersecting identities of age, racialized group, sex, and neighborhood poverty level. We also estimated the total and average financial cost associated with IE hospitalizations.

METHODS AND FINDINGS

We used hospitalization data from the HCUP AHRQ State Inpatient Database (SID) for twelve geographically and demographically diverse states (Arizona, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, Massachusetts, Minnesota, North Carolina, New Jersey, New York, Oregon, Washington, and Wisconsin) and annual 5-year American Community Survey population estimates for 2012–2021. We defined IE using ICD-9 codes (421.0, 421.1, 421.9, 036.42, 098.84, 112.81, 115.04, 115.14, or 115.94)2 and ICD-10 codes (I33, I38, I39).3

We calculated rates of IE per 100,000 population by age (18–34 and 35–64), racialized group (non-Hispanic [NH] White, Black, Asian and Pacific Islander [API], American Indian and Alaskan Native [AIAN], and Hispanic), sex (male and female), and neighborhood (proxied using zip code tabulation areas [ZCTAs]) percentage poverty (0–4.9%, 5–9.9%, 10–19.9%, and 20–100%). We restricted the study population to ages 18–65 because that is the age range where a diagnosis of IE is more likely to be associated with injection drug use. We calculated rates and 95% confidence intervals by single demographic categories as well as two-, and three-way intersecting categories across states and years. We calculated total and average cost using the cost-to-charge ratio in the SID. Across 2012–2021 in the twelve states, there were 67,420 IE hospitalizations (3.9% resulting in death) totaling $2,091,288,739 and averaging $34,537 per hospitalization.

The highest IE rates were among those aged 35–64 (10.6; 95% CI: 10.5–10.7), in ZCTAs with 20–100% poverty (12.9; 12.7–13.1), among males (11.5; 11.4–11.7) and among AIAN (17.1; 16.0–18.2) followed by NH White (11.8; 11.7–11.9) (Table 1). However, among those 18–34 years across all ZCTAs poverty levels, NH White and AIAN females had higher rates than males (14.8 [14.5–15.1] vs 10.7 [10.4–10.9] and 21.3[18.6–24.2] vs 11.4 [9.5–13.5], respectively) (Fig. 1). Regardless of sex, among those 35–64 years, in the lower poverty zip codes, Black rates were higher than NH White rates, although with overlapping CIs (0–4.9%: 6.7 [5.6–7.9] vs 6.0 [5.7–6.2] and 5–9.9%: 9.4 [8.8–10.1] vs 8.3 [8.1–8.4]) (Fig. 1).

## DISCUSSION

Our analysis highlights the substantial financial and health burden of IE (two billion dollars for 67,000 hospitalizations), and identifies three previously under recognized groups with high IE rates: 1) AIAN adults, which is likely an under count as the HCUP SID dataset excludes Indian health service hospitalizations, 2)  Black 35–64 year old adults in the lowest poverty neighborhoods, and 3) 18–34-year-old NH White and AIAN women. Most existing studies do not report IE rates among AIAN and there is little published research on IE among AIAN people. However, work that exists, shows AIANs had the highest rate of opioid overdose mortality among all racialized groups in 2022.4 Our finding of high IE rates for  Black adults aged 35–64 living in lower poverty ZCTAs is a pattern that has been seen with other outcomes.5

Two existing studies showed high rates of IE in women,6 specifically younger women,7 but these studies did not disaggregate by racialized identity. Limitations of this study include the imperfect ability of ICD codes to define IE hospitalization and reduced generalizability due to the use of only twelve states. Investigating IE hospitalization disparities using multiple sociodemographic categories revealed that disparities are heterogeneous. Understanding the burden of this costly and serious disease by multiple rather than just singular sociodemographic groups can better support tailored interventions and guide resource allocation.
